mcqs.question: Why does binary lifting store ancestors only at power-of-two distances (1, 2, 4, 8 hops...) rather than every possible distance?
options: Storing every distance would take O(n) space per node, O(n²) total, while any distance can be composed from a subset of power-of-two jumps, giving the same query capability with only O(log n) entries per node
Power-of-two distances are the only distances that occur in real trees
Storing every distance would make queries slower, not just use more space
Binary lifting only works correctly on perfect binary trees
mcqs.explanation: Any integer distance decomposes into a sum of powers of two (its binary representation), so storing just the power-of-two jumps is sufficient to reach any distance by composing a handful of them — a dramatic space reduction from O(n) to O(log n) entries per node without losing any query capability. This isn't about which distances occur naturally, storing more data wouldn't slow down queries (it's a space, not a query-speed, concern), and binary lifting works on any rooted tree, not just perfect ones.

mcqs.question: To find the ancestor 13 hops up (13 = 8 + 4 + 1 in binary), how many table lookups does the kth-ancestor query perform?
options: 13 lookups, one per hop
Exactly 3 lookups, one for each set bit in 13's binary representation (8, 4, and 1)
log(13) rounded down, regardless of how many bits are actually set
A single lookup, since the table stores every possible distance directly
mcqs.explanation: The algorithm performs one jump per set bit in k's binary representation, and 13 in binary is 1101 — three set bits (8, 4, 1) — so exactly three table lookups reach the target ancestor, not one per raw hop. It isn't simply floor(log(13)) independent of which bits are set (a different k with the same bit-length but fewer set bits would need fewer lookups), and the table doesn't store every distance directly — that's precisely what it avoids.

mcqs.question: In binary-lifting LCA, why must both nodes be brought to the same depth before the simultaneous-lifting phase begins?
options: It isn't necessary — simultaneous lifting works regardless of starting depths
Depth equalization is only needed if the tree is unbalanced
The simultaneous-lifting comparisons only make sense if both nodes are the same number of steps away from their eventual common ancestor, which requires starting from equal depth
Depth equalization improves the algorithm's time complexity from O(log n) to O(1)
mcqs.explanation: The second phase's logic — jump both nodes together whenever doing so keeps them distinct — only correctly narrows in on the LCA if both nodes are equidistant from it going in, which equal depth guarantees; without that, the comparisons between up[i][u] and up[i][v] don't reliably indicate anything about their true relationship. This is a correctness requirement for any tree shape, not merely unbalanced ones, and it doesn't change the algorithm's asymptotic complexity, which remains O(log n).

mcqs.question: An LCA implementation using binary lifting skips the depth-equalization phase and jumps straight to simultaneous lifting. What happens when the two query nodes start at different depths?
options: The algorithm still produces the correct LCA, just with extra unnecessary lookups
The algorithm throws an out-of-bounds error immediately
The result is silently wrong in the common case where the two nodes start at different depths, since the comparison logic assumes equal starting depth
The algorithm only fails if the tree has more than one root
mcqs.explanation: Without equalizing depths first, the simultaneous-lifting comparisons are being applied to nodes that aren't correctly aligned relative to their eventual common ancestor, producing a wrong answer with no error thrown — and since different-depth queries are the typical case, not a rare edge case, this bug surfaces frequently rather than occasionally. It doesn't crash with an out-of-bounds error, and it isn't related to the tree having multiple roots (a tree has exactly one).

mcqs.question: Both binary lifting and Euler tour + sparse-table RMQ solve LCA with O(n log n) preprocessing. What's the key difference between them?
options: They are functionally identical with no meaningful difference
Binary lifting only works on trees with fewer than 1000 nodes

The Euler-tour approach achieves true O(1) per query with a sparse table, strictly faster than binary lifting's O(log n), at the cost of more setup machinery; binary lifting also directly answers kth-ancestor queries, which the Euler-tour approach doesn't
Euler tour + RMQ cannot be used for LCA at all, only for range-minimum queries
mcqs.explanation: The two approaches trade off query speed against implementation complexity and query versatility: Euler-tour RMQ gets LCA down to O(1) per query but needs extra machinery and doesn't directly serve kth-ancestor queries, while binary lifting is O(log n) per query but handles both LCA and kth-ancestor with the same table. Neither is scale-limited to small trees, and Euler tour + RMQ is specifically a well-known technique for solving LCA, not merely range-minimum queries in general.
